question: What does an inverted yield curve typically signal?
before: Inverted (short > long rates) means market expects rate cuts due to economic slowdown/recession. Preceded every US recession since 1970. A describes normal/steep curve. C and D are causes not signals.
after:
Concept: An inverted yield curve occurs when short-term interest rates exceed long-term interest rates — a reversal of the normal upward-sloping curve. This inversion reflects market expectations about future economic conditions.

Why this is correct: An inverted yield curve signals that bond market participants expect slower economic growth and lower inflation ahead, prompting the central bank to cut rates. Historically, every US recession since 1970 has been preceded by a yield curve inversion, making it a reliable recession warning signal for equity analysts monitoring macroeconomic risk.

Why the others are wrong: A) Strong economic growth would produce a steep normal curve with higher long-term rates, not an inversion. B) Rising inflation alone does not cause an inversion; inflation typically steepens the curve. D) Central bank rate hikes are a cause of yield curve movements, not a signal that an inversion conveys — the inversion itself signals the opposite, that cuts are coming.

Intuition: Equity analysts use the yield curve as an early warning system for portfolio positioning. When the curve inverts, it shifts market sentiment from growth optimism to defensive positioning, often triggering a reassessment of earnings forecasts and equity valuations — particularly for cyclical stocks.
